context: The passage as a whole is best described as an account of:

choices.text: a legal dispute between siblings over an inheritance.
a woman confronting how her distance from her father shaped their relationship.
a family’s immigration from Cleveland to Dearborn.
a brother’s decision to sell the family home.

why.A: No dispute occurs; the siblings work together companionably.
why.B: Correct — the photograph and Amir’s observation drive Nadia toward recognizing her own reticence.
why.C: Immigration is background, mentioned only through the 1971 photograph.
why.D: No decision about selling is made or discussed.

context: It can reasonably be inferred that Amir’s statement "You never asked him anything" is intended to:

choices.text: accuse Nadia of deliberately neglecting their father.
observe a pattern Nadia had not recognized in herself.
defend his own decision to remain nearby.
persuade Nadia to keep the photographs.

why.A: The text explicitly says "it was not an accusation, which was what made it land."
why.B: Correct — Amir names a pattern, and the narration signals Nadia is absorbing it rather than defending herself.
why.C: Amir never justifies his own choices in the exchange.
why.D: The photographs are the occasion for the remark, not its purpose.

context: According to the passage, Amir traveled to the house from:

choices.text: Cleveland.
Ontario.
Dearborn.
the city where Nadia lived.

why.A: Cleveland is where the father arrived in 1971.
why.B: Ontario is the location of a beach in one of the photographs.
why.C: Correct — the passage states he drove ninety minutes from Dearborn every other Sunday.
why.D: Nadia’s city is never specified.

context: The detail that the house "had simply gone on being itself" primarily serves to:

choices.text: emphasize the contrast between the house’s constancy and Nadia’s own transformation.
suggest the house has been carefully maintained by Amir.
establish that the family lacked money for renovations.
foreshadow the discovery of the photograph.

why.A: Correct — the sentence directly juxtaposes "She had changed enormously" with the unchanged house.
why.B: Amir’s maintenance is mentioned later and separately; it is not the point of this line.
why.C: Finances are never raised.
why.D: Nothing in the image points toward the photograph.

context: As it is used in the fifth paragraph, "administrative" most nearly means:

choices.text: governmental.
practical and task-oriented.
authoritative.
reluctant.

why.A: No government context is present.
why.B: Correct — the following sentence lists wallpaper, boxes, and decisions about what to keep.
why.C: Nadia is not asserting authority over anyone.
why.D: Her alertness is described as arriving readily, not reluctantly.

context: The statement that "the arithmetic of it had never balanced" most strongly suggests that:

choices.text: Nadia had failed to contribute her share of household expenses.
the siblings had contributed to their father’s care in unequal and incomparable ways.
Amir had been secretly resentful for eleven years.
their father had divided his estate unfairly.

why.A: She sent money; the imbalance is not financial.
why.B: Correct — the sentence follows a list contrasting Amir’s presence with Nadia’s money and birthday calls.
why.C: The passage says neither of them ever said so, and Amir’s tone is explicitly not accusatory.
why.D: The estate’s division is never mentioned.

context: In the photograph Nadia discovers, her father is described as:

choices.text: smiling nervously beside a bus.
wearing an oversized coat and gripping a suitcase.
standing with her mother on a beach.
holding a schedule board.

why.A: The passage explicitly says he was not smiling.
why.B: Correct — "a coat too large for him" and "holding a suitcase with both hands."
why.C: That describes a different photograph in the box.
why.D: The schedule board is behind him and too blurred to read.

context: The final paragraph, describing the maple tree, primarily functions to:

choices.text: indicate that the property has become valuable.
suggest the passage of time and growth that occurred while Nadia was not paying attention.
explain why the house is difficult to heat.
introduce a new conflict between the siblings.

why.A: Property value is never at issue.
why.B: Correct — the tree Nadia "suddenly remembered" as a stick now shades the whole west side, mirroring the years she missed.
why.C: The cold under the kitchen door is a separate, earlier detail.
why.D: The passage ends without new conflict.

context: The passage draws a contrast between Nadia and Amir chiefly in terms of:

choices.text: their financial circumstances.
their affection for their father.
the form their care took — presence versus provision.
their memories of childhood.

why.A: Money appears only as one of Nadia’s contributions, not as a comparison of means.
why.B: The passage never suggests either loved the father less.
why.C: Correct — Amir drove out every other Sunday and sat through silences; Nadia sent money and fixed things.
why.D: Their childhood memories are not compared.

context: The main idea of the passage is that:

choices.text: Marchetti’s constant has been definitively disproven by recent commuting data.
a proposed regularity in travel time, though disputed, usefully reframes transportation planning around accessibility.
the fifteen-minute city is the only viable model for modern urban development.
building highways is the most effective way to reduce urban congestion.

why.A: The passage presents criticism but explicitly leaves the question "unresolved."
why.B: Correct — the passage surveys the claim, the objections, and concludes its value lies in reframing planning.
why.C: The passage notes legitimate criticisms of the fifteen-minute city.
why.D: The passage argues the opposite via induced demand.

context: According to the passage, Marchetti proposed that people tolerate a daily travel time of about:

choices.text: fifteen minutes.
thirty minutes.
one hour.
ninety minutes.

why.A: Fifteen minutes refers to the later urban design concept, not Marchetti’s figure.
why.B: Thirty minutes is each way, not the daily total.
why.C: Correct — "roughly one hour of travel per day — about thirty minutes each way."
why.D: Ninety minutes is cited as an extreme in the range of U.S. commutes.

context: The examples of medieval walking villages and nineteenth-century streetcar suburbs primarily serve to:

choices.text: demonstrate that cities were healthier before automobiles.
illustrate the claim that faster travel yields greater distance rather than saved time.
argue that streetcars should be reintroduced.
establish the chronology of European urban development.

why.A: Health is never discussed.
why.B: Correct — both examples show settlements expanding to a new radius that still takes about thirty minutes to cross.
why.C: No policy recommendation about streetcars is made.
why.D: Chronology is incidental to the argument.

context: The passage suggests that the observation "what looks like a stable preference may in some cases be a stable constraint" implies that:

choices.text: some long commutes reflect limited housing options rather than willing choice.
commuters consistently underestimate how long their trips take.
travel surveys are generally unreliable.
people prefer longer commutes than Marchetti assumed.

why.A: Correct — the preceding sentence describes commuters "priced out of the neighborhoods near their jobs."
why.B: Estimation error is never raised.
why.C: The critique concerns which populations the data draw on, not the surveys’ accuracy.
why.D: The point is that some travel more than they would prefer.

context: The 2011 study of American metropolitan areas is cited as evidence that:

choices.text: commute times have risen since 1980.
new lane capacity is absorbed by additional driving, leaving congestion largely unchanged.
transit investment outperforms highway investment.
remote work reduces total vehicle miles traveled.

why.A: That claim is supported by different figures, from 1980 and 2019.
why.B: Correct — vehicle miles traveled rose "almost exactly in proportion to new lane miles built."
why.C: No comparison to transit investment is made.
why.D: Remote work is discussed only in the final paragraph, with ambiguous results.

context: As used in the fifth paragraph, "accessibility" most nearly means:

choices.text: accommodation for people with disabilities.
how much a person can reach within a given travel time.
the affordability of housing near transit.
the ease of obtaining a driver’s license.

why.A: A common meaning of the word, but not the planning sense used here.
why.B: Correct — the paragraph defines it as what people "can reach within the time they are already willing to spend."
why.C: Affordability appears later as a criticism, not as this definition.
why.D: Irrelevant to the passage.

context: The passage characterizes the fifteen-minute city as "Marchetti’s inverted" because it:

choices.text: rejects the idea that travel time is stable.
takes the travel budget as fixed and asks what can be brought within it, rather than how far it extends.
seeks to reduce the travel time budget below thirty minutes.
applies only to European cities.

why.A: It relies on that stability rather than rejecting it.
why.B: Correct — the final sentence of that paragraph states this contrast explicitly.
why.C: The model concerns what is reachable, not shortening the budget itself.
why.D: The passage notes questions about non-European application but does not define the concept that way.

context: The author’s attitude toward Marchetti’s constant is best described as:

choices.text: enthusiastic endorsement of it as a natural law.
qualified interest in its usefulness despite unresolved objections.
dismissal of it as an outdated hypothesis.
indifference to the debate surrounding it.

why.A: The author writes that "not everyone accepts" it and calls the question unresolved.
why.B: Correct — the author presents criticisms fairly while arguing its "practical value does not depend on its being a law."
why.C: The author explicitly defends its usefulness.
why.D: The passage engages the debate in detail.

context: The passage indicates that early data on remote work are ambiguous because some remote workers have:

choices.text: returned to full-time office schedules.
moved farther away and now travel longer on office days, keeping weekly totals similar.
relocated to dense fifteen-minute neighborhoods.
stopped commuting entirely.

why.A: A return to full-time office work is not described.
why.B: Correct — the final paragraph states exactly this pattern.
why.C: No such relocation is reported.
why.D: The passage describes them as still traveling on some days.

context: The main purpose of Passage A is to:

choices.text: argue that digital restoration is a necessary rescue rather than an optional enhancement.
catalogue the chemical processes by which film stock decays.
criticize audiences who prefer unrestored prints.
propose new funding for film archives.

why.A: Correct — the archivist frames decay as an arithmetic certainty and restoration as rescue, while conceding that judgment is involved.
why.B: Decay is described in the opening but serves the argument rather than being the point.
why.C: The author expresses "some sympathy" for that objection.
why.D: Funding is never mentioned.

context: According to Passage A, a scratch inflicted by a projectionist in 1958 should be regarded as:

choices.text: part of the film’s historical texture that must be preserved.
damage that is not part of the film’s history and may properly be removed.
evidence of the film’s popularity.
impossible to remove with current software.

why.A: The author explicitly rejects this position.
why.B: Correct — "A tear introduced by a careless projectionist in 1958 tells us about that projectionist, not about the film."
why.C: Popularity is never invoked.
why.D: The passage describes removing exactly such damage.

context: The author of Passage B would most likely respond to Passage A’s claim that restorations should be "documented, reversible, and modest" by:

choices.text: rejecting it as insufficient because restoration should be halted entirely.
agreeing with it and noting that such documentation rarely reaches ordinary viewers.
dismissing it as irrelevant to questions of grain and color.
arguing that archives should not preserve raw scans.

why.A: Passage B states plainly, "I do not want restoration halted."
why.B: Correct — B’s central complaint is that judgments "arrive invisibly" to streaming viewers, and asks only that they be labeled.
why.C: Documentation is precisely B’s remedy for the grain and color problems.
why.D: B never opposes preserving raw scans.

context: Passage B objects to aggressive noise reduction primarily because it:

choices.text: makes films more expensive to restore.
removes grain that constitutes the physical substrate of the image, producing a look no original audience saw.
introduces new scratches into the image.
cannot be applied consistently across a full film.

why.A: Cost is never discussed.
why.B: Correct — B calls grain "the physical substrate of the image" and the smoothed result "technically sharper and historically falser."
why.C: Noise reduction removes rather than adds damage.
why.D: Consistency is not the objection raised.

context: Both passages agree that:

choices.text: restoration inevitably involves interpretive judgment.
grain should be preserved at all costs.
streaming platforms have improved access to film history.
no single original version of a color film exists.

why.A: Correct — A concedes "restoration involves judgment," and B’s entire argument concerns the invisibility of those judgments.
why.B: Only B makes grain central; A does not address it.
why.C: B treats streaming as part of the problem; A does not discuss it.
why.D: Only B makes this claim about Technicolor prints.

context: The chief difference between the two passages is that Passage A emphasizes ____, while Passage B emphasizes ____.

choices.text: the urgency of physical decay ... the invisibility of restorers’ interpretive choices
the cost of restoration ... the aesthetics of grain
the history of nitrate film ... the economics of streaming
audience preferences ... archival technique

why.A: Correct — A opens with "Every film print is dying"; B’s stated concern is that judgments "arrive invisibly."
why.B: Neither passage discusses cost.
why.C: Streaming economics are never analyzed.
why.D: This reverses both passages’ actual emphases.

context: As used in the final paragraph of Passage B, "settle for" most nearly means:

choices.text: pay compensation for.
be satisfied with.
resolve a dispute about.
establish residence in.

why.A: No payment is involved.
why.B: Correct — the author says he would accept less than the archivist expects: labeling rather than halting.
why.C: "Settle" alone can mean this, but "settle for" does not.
why.D: Irrelevant to the sentence.

context: The reference to restorations that were "quietly revised after this criticism" serves to:

choices.text: suggest that the concern about noise reduction is shared within the profession.
accuse restorers of concealing their methods deliberately.
demonstrate that digital restoration is technically unreliable.
introduce the discussion of Technicolor.

why.A: Correct — B notes it "suggests the concern is not merely nostalgic," citing professional revision as evidence.
why.B: "Quietly" indicates low profile, not deliberate concealment; B’s complaint is about labeling to viewers.
why.C: The point concerns aesthetic judgment, not technical failure.
why.D: Technicolor is introduced in the next paragraph by a separate transition.

context: It can be inferred that the author of Passage A includes the concession about judgment in order to:

choices.text: abandon the argument for restoration.
strengthen the argument by acknowledging its limits before rejecting the alternative.
agree with critics that restoration should be delayed.
explain why color timing is impossible.

why.A: The paragraph ends by rejecting inaction as preserving "nothing at all."
why.B: Correct — this is a classic concession that builds credibility before the final rebuttal.
why.C: A argues delay costs irrecoverable frames.
why.D: A treats color timing as interpretive, not impossible.

context: The passage is primarily concerned with:

choices.text: explaining how hydrophone networks are constructed.
describing the shared, changing nature of humpback song and the competing explanations for it.
arguing that humpback whales possess language comparable to human speech.
documenting the decline of humpback populations in the South Pacific.

why.A: Hydrophones appear only as a method in one paragraph.
why.B: Correct — the passage establishes the shared-and-shifting song, then surveys three hypotheses.
why.C: The passage compares song to culture and fashion, never to language.
why.D: Population decline is never mentioned.

context: According to the passage, humpback song was first described by researchers in:

choices.text: the 1950s.

why.A: Correct — "since Roger and Katy Payne first described humpback song in 1971."
why.B: That year belongs to the Marchetti paper in a different passage.
why.C: 1996 is when the novel song arrived off eastern Australia.
why.D: No 1950s date appears.

context: The 1996 event off eastern Australia is significant because the local population:

choices.text: gradually modified its existing song over several seasons.
abandoned its own song and adopted a distinct song from a distant population.
ceased singing entirely for two years.
split into two groups with different songs.

why.A: That describes ordinary within-season change, not the 1996 event.
why.B: Correct — within two years the eastern population "adopted the western one wholesale."
why.C: Singing did not stop.
why.D: No split is described; the replacement was population-wide.

context: The passage suggests that a simple "advertisement of male quality" explanation is problematic because:

choices.text: females have not been observed responding to song.
a signal identical across all competitors cannot distinguish among individuals.
only older males sing.
song occurs primarily on feeding grounds rather than breeding grounds.

why.A: Female response is not the stated objection.
why.B: Correct — the passage states that such a signal "conveys nothing about any individual."
why.C: Age is never discussed.
why.D: The passage says males sing chiefly on the breeding grounds.

context: The "novelty" hypothesis described in the passage would explain:

choices.text: why only males sing.
both the constant change in song and its rapid adoption.
why songs travel from east to west.
why song complexity decreases over time.

why.A: The hypothesis concerns female preference for new variants, not the sex of singers.
why.B: Correct — the passage says it "would explain both the constant change and the rapid adoption."
why.C: The documented direction is westward-origin moving eastward.
why.D: The passage reports complexity increasing until a new song arrives.

context: The final sentence’s comparison of whale song to "the behavior of a fashion" primarily functions to:

choices.text: argue that whales imitate human cultural practices.
characterize the observed cycle of elaboration followed by wholesale replacement.
dismiss the scientific significance of the findings.
introduce a new hypothesis about female choice.

why.A: No claim of imitation of humans is made.
why.B: Correct — the sentence follows the finding that songs grow elaborate, then are replaced when a new one arrives.
why.C: The author calls the finding one that "complicates the picture usefully."
why.D: It offers an analogy, not a fourth hypothesis.

context: As used in the passage, "propagate" most nearly means:

choices.text: reproduce biologically.
spread through the population.
become louder.
be recorded.

why.A: A common meaning of the word, but the sentence concerns song changes, not breeding.
why.B: Correct — the next sentence explains that every male adopts the changes within weeks.
why.C: Volume is not discussed.
why.D: Recording is a research method described later.

context: It can be inferred that passive acoustic monitoring is valuable to researchers chiefly because it:

choices.text: allows song to be tracked across ocean basins without disturbing the animals.
produces higher-quality recordings than earlier methods.
identifies individual whales by name.
eliminates the need for machine-learning analysis.

why.A: Correct — the passage notes whales "cannot be marked without considerable disturbance" and that hydrophones track songs "without observing the singers at all."
why.B: Recording quality is never compared.
why.C: The passage says individuals are difficult to identify.
why.D: Machine learning is described as handling the sorting, not being replaced.

context: The "population marker" hypothesis differs from the "coordination" hypothesis in that only the former:

choices.text: assigns the song a role in identifying members of the same breeding group.
assumes females play no role in selection.
accounts for the song’s annual changes.
relies on acoustic monitoring data.

why.A: Correct — the population-marker hypothesis is defined by conspecific identification; the coordination hypothesis concerns spacing and readiness among males.
why.B: Both de-emphasize direct female attraction; that is not what distinguishes them.
why.C: Neither is presented as primarily explaining annual change; that is the novelty hypothesis.
why.D: Monitoring is a method common to all research described.

context: The passage is best described as an account of:

choices.text: a bank’s decision to stop lending to small businesses.
a narrator coming to understand why the mother’s finances were never only financial.
a family’s decision to sell the bakery.
the economic history of a coastal town.

why.A: Mr. Callan grants the loan every year.
why.B: Correct — the narrator moves from criticizing the arithmetic to grasping what the mother was also counting.
why.C: No sale is discussed.
why.D: The town is background, not the subject.

context: According to the passage, the narrator was how old when accompanying the mother to the bank?

choices.text: Fifteen
Nineteen
Twenty-three
Thirty-nine

why.A: The age at which the narrator was first right about the arithmetic.
why.B: Correct — "when I was nineteen and had opinions."
why.C: No such age appears.
why.D: Not stated; roughly twenty years have passed since.

context: The detail that Mr. Callan asks after a grandmother who has been dead six years most strongly suggests that:

choices.text: he is not aware of her death.
the exchange is a ritual whose purpose is connection rather than information.
the mother is deceiving him about her circumstances.
he is close to retirement.

why.A: The narrator later says Callan knew she was dead.
why.B: Correct — the passage calls it "part of it too," and the closing paragraph names it as one of the other things being counted.
why.C: The deception reading is contradicted by "a woman he knew was dead."
why.D: Nothing indicates his career stage.

context: The sentence "She listened to all of it without interrupting, which should have warned me" primarily serves to:

choices.text: show that the mother agreed with the narrator’s analysis.
signal, in hindsight, that the mother had a reply the narrator had not anticipated.
establish that the mother was distracted by driving.
introduce a conflict that ends the relationship.

why.A: She does partly agree, but that is not what the warning refers to.
why.B: Correct — "should have warned me" is retrospective narration flagging what follows.
why.C: No distraction is described.
why.D: No rupture occurs.

context: As used in the passage, "counting" most nearly means:

choices.text: reciting numbers aloud.
taking into account as part of the decision.
depending on someone for help.
expecting an outcome.

why.A: No literal counting occurs.
why.B: Correct — the mother weighs non-financial factors alongside the arithmetic.
why.C: That would be "counting on."
why.D: Also "counting on," a different idiom.

context: The passage indicates that the bakery sold bread at a loss during the winter because:

choices.text: the flour supplier raised prices.
closing for the winter would have meant not reopening in summer.
the fishing crews refused to pay.
a competitor had opened nearby.

why.A: Supply costs are never mentioned.
why.B: Correct — "if she closed the door in November it would not open in June."
why.C: No refusal to pay is described.
why.D: No competitor appears.

context: Mr. Callan’s remark about February is directed at the narrator rather than the mother most likely because:

choices.text: the mother had asked him to explain the loan.
he recognized that the narrator was the one who needed the reason spelled out.
he was avoiding eye contact with the mother.
the narrator had asked him a direct question.

why.A: No such request is described.
why.B: Correct — the narrator has just argued the arithmetic is insane, and Callan supplies the counting the narrator is missing.
why.C: No such detail appears.
why.D: The narrator only shakes his hand.

context: The narrator at nineteen differs from the narrator telling the story chiefly in:

choices.text: understanding what the mother was weighing beyond profit.
ability to perform arithmetic.
affection for the mother.
knowledge of the town’s history.

why.A: Correct — the closing paragraph describes twenty years of working out what she meant.
why.B: The arithmetic was correct then and now.
why.C: No change in affection is indicated.
why.D: The town is equally familiar to both.

context: The final sentence functions primarily to:

choices.text: concede that the mother’s business model was unsustainable.
reverse the narrator’s earlier framing by making the human factors the point of the ledger.
explain how the loan was eventually repaid.
introduce a new character.

why.A: The narrator never retracts the arithmetic, but that is not the sentence’s work.
why.B: Correct — it states that these factors were "the actual reason the ledger existed," not additions to it.
why.C: Repayment is never resolved.
why.D: No new character appears.

context: The main idea of the passage is that:

choices.text: Elisha Gray deserves credit for inventing the telephone.
simultaneous invention is common, which complicates how societies reward invention.
patents should be abolished in all industries.
individual brilliance plays no role in technological progress.

why.A: Gray opens the passage as an illustration, not its subject.
why.B: Correct — the passage documents the pattern and then traces its implications for patents.
why.C: The passage says a uniform regime is unlikely to be optimal, not that patents should end.
why.D: It explicitly says brilliance is relocated, not denied.

context: Ogburn and Thomas catalogued how many cases of simultaneous invention?

why.A: Not a figure in the passage.
why.B: Not a figure in the passage.
why.C: Correct — the passage states 148 cases.
why.D: This is the year Bell filed his patent.

context: The mention of Helmholtz and the telegraph industry serves primarily to:

choices.text: prove Bell plagiarized his design.
identify the prior conditions that made the telephone solvable.
explain how patents are filed.
compare European and American research.

why.A: No plagiarism is alleged.
why.B: Correct — they are given as the prerequisites that put Bell in "a room that many people had entered."
why.C: Filing procedure is not described.
why.D: No such comparison is drawn.

context: It can be inferred that a defender of the patent system would most likely respond to the simultaneity argument by claiming that:

choices.text: simultaneous invention has never occurred.
the prospect of a monopoly is what drives the costly final effort.
inventions are entirely determined by prior conditions.
prizes are always superior to patents.

why.A: The passage treats the pattern as well documented.
why.B: Correct — the passage attributes exactly this reply to patent defenders.
why.C: That is the argument they are resisting.
why.D: That is the opposing position.

context: According to the passage, studies of pharmaceuticals suggest that:

choices.text: weak patent protection still produces substantial innovation.
strong patent protection matters where development costs are high and copying is easy.
patents have no measurable effect.
prizes outperform patents.

why.A: That describes the nineteenth-century exhibition studies.
why.B: Correct — the passage says pharmaceutical studies "find the opposite."
why.C: The passage reports an effect in that sector.
why.D: No such comparison is reported for pharmaceuticals.

context: As used in the passage, "relocates" most nearly means:

choices.text: moves to a new physical address.
reassigns to a different place in the explanation.
eliminates entirely.
measures precisely.

why.A: No physical movement is described.
why.B: Correct — brilliance is repositioned within a causal account rather than removed.
why.C: The sentence explicitly says it does not deny brilliance.
why.D: Nothing is being measured.

context: The passage suggests that a patent monopoly may "retard the very diffusion it was designed to encourage" because it:

choices.text: restricts use of a solution that others would have reached anyway.
requires inventors to publish their methods.
is too short in duration.
applies only to pharmaceuticals.

why.A: Correct — if timing rather than creation is rewarded, the monopoly blocks others who were nearly there.
why.B: Publication would aid diffusion, not retard it.
why.C: Duration is never discussed.
why.D: Pharmaceuticals are one example among several.

context: The final paragraph functions primarily to:

choices.text: propose a specific reform to patent law.
explain why the inaccurate story survives despite the evidence.
summarize the studies cited earlier.
introduce a new case of simultaneous invention.

why.A: No reform is proposed there.
why.B: Correct — it argues the lone-inventor story persists because it is useful, not because it is true.
why.C: The studies are not revisited.
why.D: No new case appears.

context: The passage contrasts the popular telling of the Bell–Gray story with the historians’ telling chiefly in that historians treat the coincidence as:

choices.text: evidence of fraud.
typical rather than exceptional.
a legal dispute.
an unimportant detail.

why.A: Fraud is never suggested.
why.B: Correct — "the simultaneity is not the anomaly. It is the pattern."
why.C: The patent conflict is background, not the historians’ point.
why.D: They treat it as highly significant.

context: The passage is primarily concerned with:

choices.text: the medical treatment of focal dystonia.
how relearning an instrument after injury changed the author’s understanding of playing.
arguing that musicians should practice less.
the author’s early career successes.

why.A: The passage notes there is almost no useful treatment and moves on.
why.B: Correct — the arc runs from loss to relearning to a different kind of understanding.
why.C: The reduced practice is a constraint of the author’s situation, not a general prescription.
why.D: Early success occupies one sentence.

context: According to the passage, focal dystonia is:

choices.text: painful and treatable.
painless but effectively disabling for a musician.
caused by a single injury to the tendon.
reversible with rest.

why.A: The passage says it is painless and has almost no useful treatment.
why.B: Correct — "It is painless. It is also, for a musician, absolute."
why.C: It is described as neurological, not tendon damage.
why.D: No reversal is described.

context: The author found the neurologist’s explanation "clarifying" most likely because it:

choices.text: offered a cure.
identified sameness of movement as the cause, which suggested how to practice differently.
proved the injury was not the author’s fault.
showed the condition was common among violinists.

why.A: No cure is offered anywhere in the passage.
why.B: Correct — the author later says "sameness was now the enemy" and varies everything.
why.C: The explanation implicates the author’s own practice, and blame is never the issue.
why.D: Prevalence is never mentioned.

context: The author’s second period of learning differed from the first in that it relied on:

choices.text: imitation and long hours.
analysis, variation, and limited practice time.
a different teacher.
a smaller instrument.

why.A: That describes the first learning at age nine.

why.C: No teacher is mentioned.
why.D: The instrument was restrung, not resized.

context: As used in the passage, "absolute" most nearly means:

choices.text: perfect.
total in its effect.
certain to be diagnosed.
unrelated to other conditions.

why.A: Nothing is being praised as perfect.

why.C: Diagnosis is not the subject of the sentence.

context: The comparison of the lost skill to "a rented thing" primarily conveys:

choices.text: the financial cost of the author’s training.
the shock of discovering that something felt innate was contingent.
that the author had borrowed the instrument.
that the skill would eventually return.

why.B: Correct — the skill had felt like a property of the body, "like being right-handed," until it was revoked.

context: The author anticipates that the closing claim may sound like "consolation" and denies it. This suggests the author believes:

choices.text: the second learning produced a real gain, not merely a comforting story.
readers will not believe the injury occurred.
the technical loss was insignificant.
other musicians should injure themselves.

context: The passage suggests that the first learning and the second differed most fundamentally in:

choices.text: which hand was used.
whether the process was examined or taken for granted.
the genre of music studied.
the author’s level of talent.

why.A: True but presented as the occasion, not the fundamental difference.

context: How long did it take the author to reach, left-handed, a level passed at thirteen on the original side?

choices.text: Two years
Nine years
Fourteen years
Twenty-six years

why.A: The period spent finding the explanation unbearable.

why.C: The length of the original training.

context: The passage is primarily concerned with:

choices.text: proving that senescent cells cause all aging.
how understanding of cellular senescence evolved and why clearing these cells is promising but cautious.
the biography of Leonard Hayflick.
arguing that senolytic drugs should be approved immediately.

why.B: Correct — it traces the Hayflick limit through telomeres, the secretory phenotype, and senolytics with caveats.

context: According to the passage, telomeres:

choices.text: cause cells to divide indefinitely.
cap chromosomes and shorten with each division.
are produced by senescent cells.
were discovered by Alexis Carrel.

context: The passage states that senescent cells:

choices.text: die immediately after their final division.
stop dividing but remain alive and secrete signaling molecules.
continue dividing at a slower rate.
are found only in elderly animals.

why.B: Correct — they permanently stop dividing and produce the secretory phenotype.
why.C: Division stops entirely.
why.D: They are produced continuously in young animals as well.

context: It can be inferred that researchers pursued clearing senescent cells rather than preventing senescence because prevention would:

choices.text: be technically impossible.
remove a mechanism that protects against cancer.
require gene editing in humans.
shorten telomeres further.

why.A: Impossibility is never claimed.
why.B: Correct — the passage notes senescence "is also a defense against cancer."
why.C: Gene editing is mentioned only for the engineered mice.
why.D: Prevention would not shorten telomeres.

context: The reference to Alexis Carrel’s contaminated experiment serves to:

choices.text: explain why cells were wrongly believed to be immortal before 1961.
demonstrate that senescence protects against cancer.
introduce the secretory phenotype.
describe an early senolytic trial.

why.A: Correct — the belief rested "largely on a contaminated experiment."
why.B: That point arises much later and from different evidence.
why.C: The phenotype appears in a later paragraph.
why.D: Senolytic trials came decades afterward.

context: As used in the passage, "indication" most nearly means:

choices.text: a sign or hint.
a medical condition a treatment is approved to address.
a measurement.
a warning label.

why.A: A common sense of the word, but not the regulatory usage here.
why.B: Correct — the sentence concerns regulators not recognizing aging as a treatable condition.
why.C: Nothing is being measured.
why.D: No labeling is discussed.

context: The passage suggests that the senescence-associated secretory phenotype is best described as:

choices.text: uniformly harmful.
beneficial in the short term and harmful when sustained.
irrelevant to aging.
a product of telomere lengthening.

why.A: It aids wound healing and immune recruitment.
why.B: Correct — useful "in small numbers and for short periods," damaging when cells accumulate over years.
why.C: It is central to the passage’s account of aging.
why.D: It follows telomere shortening, not lengthening.

context: Early human trials of senolytics have targeted:

choices.text: aging itself.
specific conditions such as pulmonary fibrosis and diabetic kidney disease.
cancer prevention.
wound healing.

why.A: The passage says regulators do not recognize aging as an indication.

why.C: Cancer appears as a caution, not a trial target.
why.D: Wound healing is raised as a risk of clearing, not a target.

context: The closing sentence, "It is how many, where, and when," primarily serves to:

choices.text: reject senolytics as unworkable.
reframe the issue from whether these cells are harmful to how precisely they must be managed.
summarize the mouse results.
call for faster regulatory approval.

why.A: The passage reports substantial promise.
why.B: Correct — it replaces a yes/no framing with questions of dose, location, and timing.
why.C: Mouse results appear earlier and are not restated.
why.D: The paragraph argues for caution instead.

context: The example comparing "an hour of accounting advice and an hour of yard work" in the first paragraph primarily functions to—

choices.text: prove that accounting advice is objectively less valuable than yard work.
introduce the critics who argue that time banks fail to scale to full neighborhood economies.
explain why some time banks choose to exclude licensed trades from their exchanges.
illustrate concretely what the time bank's flat, hour-for-hour equivalence actually means in practice.

why.D: This early example makes the abstract idea of flat hour-for-hour value concrete, before the passage moves on to discuss administration and critics.
why.A: the passage makes no claim about the objective value of either service
why.B: the critics are introduced in a later paragraph, not through this example
why.C: that explanation appears in a later paragraph and is not connected to this specific comparison

context: The sentence "What mattered, Master Alduin often said, was that a chart carried his name" primarily functions in the passage to—

choices.text: prove that Master Alduin's charts were more accurate than those of his professional rivals.
explain the personal stakes that make Master Alduin resistant to being corrected.
foreshadow that Master Alduin will eventually dismiss Mireille from her apprenticeship.
provide historical background on how the shipping company was originally founded.

why.B: This sentence gives the reader Master Alduin's own stated reasoning for why he resists correction - his name and reputation are on the line - which explains both his treatment of the journeyman and Mireille's fear of confronting him.
why.A: the sentence is about his attitude toward his reputation, not a comparison to other cartographers
why.C: the passage's ending contradicts this - he keeps her on and extends her more responsibility
why.D: the sentence is about Master Alduin's personal values, not the shipping company's history

context: The sentence "Understood in isolation, holding a seed hostage to fire looks like poor design. Understood against the specific ecology of a fire-adapted forest, it looks instead like the only design that reliably works" primarily functions in the passage to—

choices.text: summarize the passage's overall conclusion after all of its supporting evidence has been presented.
introduce a competing scientific theory that the rest of the passage will go on to refute.
signal a shift from describing serotiny's apparent costs to explaining the ecological logic that justifies it.
prove that serotinous trees are more intelligent than non-serotinous conifer species.

why.C: This sentence pivots the passage from the apparent evolutionary gamble of serotiny to the detailed ecological explanation that occupies the remaining paragraphs.
why.A: this sentence appears early, before most of the supporting evidence, functioning as a transition rather than a final summary
why.B: no competing theory is introduced or refuted anywhere in the passage
why.D: the passage never makes any claim about tree intelligence

context: The sentence "That was the whole of the job, Master Okafor liked to say. Not the flame. The turning." primarily functions in the passage to—

choices.text: reveal that Master Okafor considers the flame itself unimportant to the lighthouse's function.
explain why Renata was initially denied permission to stand a solo watch.
foreshadow that the lighthouse will eventually be replaced by an automated system.
establish, early on, the specific mechanical detail that will become central to the story's crisis later that night.

why.D: By naming the turning, rather than the flame, as the real job, this early sentence sets up the gear failure that becomes the passage's central problem.
why.A: overstates his view - he is drawing a distinction of emphasis, not calling the flame unimportant
why.B: unrelated to the four-month wait mentioned in the opening sentence
why.C: no such topic appears anywhere in the passage

context: The comparison to a building whose 'materials...age faster than the design they were meant to serve' primarily functions in the passage to—

choices.text: argue that older translations should be physically discarded rather than kept in print.
suggest that translators need formal training in architecture to do their work well.
clarify why retranslation should be understood as ongoing maintenance rather than as a correction of past mistakes.
prove that all buildings and all translations eventually fail in the same way.

why.C: This comparison directly follows the sentence stating 'retranslation is not vanity in this light; it is maintenance,' clarifying that idea with a concrete parallel.
why.A: no such argument about discarding older translations is made
why.B: the architecture reference is a comparison, not a claim about translator training
why.D: overstates the comparison into a universal claim the passage never makes

context: The description of the note app opening 'by accident...into an email I meant to answer three days ago' in Passage A primarily functions to—

choices.text: criticize a specific email application by name for its poor design.
explain why the author originally chose to start keeping a journal at all.
give a concrete, personal example of the kind of distraction the author believes a paper notebook eliminates.
suggest that the author has generally poor time-management skills.

why.C: This specific, embarrassing example makes concrete the paragraph's broader claim that a notebook 'cannot open, by accident, into some other application entirely.'
why.A: no specific application is named in the passage
why.B: this detail illustrates a drawback of phone journaling, not the author's original motivation for journaling
why.D: the detail is offered as an example of the tool's distraction, not as a broader claim about the author's habits

context: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the passage?

choices.text: It explains how time banks work and the reasoning behind them, then examines the factors that determine whether a given time bank succeeds or fails.
It presents two opposing historical accounts of when time banking first began, then resolves the disagreement.
It narrates, in chronological order, the founding and eventual collapse of one specific time bank.
It opens with a critic's objection and spends the remainder of the passage refuting it point by point.

why.A: The passage moves from defining the time-bank concept and its motivation to analyzing the administrative and social factors that separate lasting banks from failing ones.
why.B: no competing historical origin accounts appear anywhere in the passage
why.C: the passage discusses time banks in general terms, not the history of one specific bank
why.D: the passage does not open with an objection, and it does not simply refute the critics it later discusses

context: Which choice best describes the relationship between the passage's fourth and fifth paragraphs?

The two paragraphs describe two entirely unrelated adaptations found in different pine species.
The fourth paragraph is a historical account, and the fifth paragraph is a prediction about the future.
The fourth paragraph explains an advantage of synchronized germination, and the fifth paragraph identifies a cost that emerges from that same synchronization.

why.D: The fourth paragraph explains why synchronized germination benefits a new generation of seedlings, and the fifth paragraph turns to the forest-scale cost of that same synchronization.
why.A: no experiment or disproof is described in the fifth paragraph
why.B: both paragraphs concern the same synchronized-germination adaptation in serotinous pines
why.C: neither paragraph is framed as history or as a future prediction

context: The tone of the passage's final paragraph is best described as—

choices.text: quietly admiring, treating Renata's competence as noteworthy even though Master Okafor himself does not say so directly.
openly celebratory, matching the harbor office's enthusiastic reaction to the news.
bitterly ironic, mocking Master Okafor's inability to praise his assistant properly.
coldly clinical, focused only on the technical details of the gear replacement.

why.A: The paragraph's focus on how Renata comes to understand his understated words as a genuine compliment gives it a quietly admiring tone.
why.B: the harbor office's reaction is never described as enthusiastic
why.C: the paragraph is sincere, not ironic or mocking
why.D: the paragraph focuses on what his words meant to Renata, not on technical detail

context: The tone of the passage toward the practice of retranslating classic novels is best described as—

choices.text: dismissive, treating retranslation as a wasteful publishing gimmick.
nostalgic, longing for a return to nineteenth-century translation standards.
alarmed, warning readers that most modern translations cannot be trusted.
measured and analytical, treating retranslation as a reasonable response to real linguistic and interpretive change.

why.D: Across all three of its supporting reasons, the passage explains retranslation calmly and even-handedly, including a fair hearing of its critics, which gives it a measured, analytical tone.
why.A: contradicted - the passage takes retranslation seriously as 'maintenance,' not waste
why.B: the passage explains why earlier standards became dated rather than idealizing them
why.C: no alarm or warning of this kind appears in the passage

context: As it is used in the passage, the word "smooth" in the phrase "her explanation rehearsed so many times it had worn smooth" most nearly means—

choices.text: practiced until it flowed without hesitation.
physically flat and even in texture.
calm and even-tempered in manner.
polished to a glossy shine.

why.A: The passage uses "worn smooth" figuratively, the way repeated handling wears an object smooth, to describe an explanation Mireille has rehearsed so many times that it comes out fluently, without stumbling.
why.B: the literal, physical meaning of "smooth," not the figurative meaning used here
why.C: describes a personality trait, not the rehearsed quality of an explanation
why.D: another literal, physical sense of the word that doesn't fit an explanation being described

choices.text: a physical book bound in leather, used for older accounting methods.
a formal record that tracks what each member has given and is owed.
a legal contract that obligates a member to repay a debt.
a public announcement of a time bank's rules to new members.

why.A: the literal, physical sense of the word, not how it functions in this passage's discussion
why.C: overstates the term - the passage treats a deficit as trust-based, not a binding legal contract
why.D: confuses the ledger with a set of rules, which the passage discusses separately

context: As it is used in the passage, the word "stilted" in the fourth paragraph most nearly means—

choices.text: elevated on physical supports, as a building might be.
deliberately funny in a way that is out of place.
exceptionally rich in figurative language and imagery.
unnaturally stiff and awkward in phrasing.

why.D: The passage uses "stilted" to describe sentences produced by a translation aiming at maximum literal precision - stiff, awkward English rather than natural prose.
why.A: the literal, architectural sense of the word, not the sense used to describe prose here
why.B: conflates 'stilted' with 'comic,' a different quality raised elsewhere in the passage

a small committee formed to manage a shared forest resource.
a single tree that produces an unusually large number of cones.
a species of insect that feeds specifically on pine seedlings.

why.A: The passage uses "cohort" to describe the group of trees that germinated together after the same fire and therefore ages, matures, and becomes vulnerable together.
why.B: confuses the ecological sense of the word with an administrative sense
why.C: the term describes a group of trees, not an individual tree's cone production
why.D: no such insect is mentioned anywhere in the passage

context: The main function of the third paragraph is to:

choices.text: explain why a reasonable objection was raised and how evidence finally answered it.
demonstrate that the critics of the partnership theory were motivated by professional rivalry.
introduce the chemical processes that allow lichens to break down rock.
compare the growth of a lichen with the growth of a moss.

context: Which choice best describes how the passage handles the claim that multiplying translations benefits readers?

It presents the claim's reasoning, then raises a genuine counterobjection without fully settling which side is correct.
It ignores any possible objection to the claim entirely.

Passage B contradicts itself by claiming that digital notes are both searchable and difficult to organize.

Passage B does not fully address Passage A's claim that the effort required by handwriting improves the quality of a reflection before it is even written, focusing instead on access after the fact.

context: Which choice best characterizes the relationship between the personal anecdotes used in Passage A and in Passage B?

Passage A uses a family member's experience, while Passage B uses the author's own habit, to make opposite arguments from what each actually makes.
Passage A uses the author's own notebook habit to argue for paper's benefits, while Passage B uses a family member's notebooks to argue for paper's practical limitations.

why.B: swaps which anecdote belongs to which passage
why.D: both passages clearly rely on personal anecdotes - the author's own notebooks in A, the grandmother's diary in B

context: A reader who accepted the reasoning in both Passage A and Passage B fully would most likely conclude that—

choices.text: digital note-taking is entirely without value for personal reflection.
handwriting guarantees a permanent record that will always remain readable to future generations.
there is no meaningful difference between the two methods once friction is set aside.
handwriting may improve the quality of individual reflections, but a digital system may better preserve access to those reflections over many years.

why.D: Combining Passage A's case for handwriting's filtering effect with Passage B's case for digital access over decades produces a synthesis in which each method offers a distinct advantage.

why.B: contradicted by Passage B's account of the grandmother's largely inaccessible diary
why.C: both passages describe meaningful differences beyond friction, such as searchability and tagging

choices.text: An hour of teaching bicycle repair earns the same credit as an hour of gardening.
Some time banks exclude licensed trades like electrical work from their exchanges.
Banks organized among people who already saw each other at a community center or shared block tend to survive slow patches better than banks assembled from online sign-ups.

Foresters have begun observing land that burns and then fails to regrow the same forest it burned away.

why.C: supports the description of the resin threshold, not the claim about shortened fire intervals

context: Both passages are primarily concerned with—

choices.text: describing the biographical details of the authors' family members.
comparing the practice of handwritten journaling to digital note-taking as tools for personal reflection.
arguing that one specific journaling app is superior to all its competitors.
explaining the history of the notebook as a manufactured object.

why.B: Both authors compare their own experience of handwritten and digital journaling to make a broader case for one method's advantages for personal reflection.
why.A: the grandmother is mentioned only in Passage B, and only briefly, not as the main concern of either passage
why.C: neither passage names or promotes a specific app
why.D: neither passage discusses the manufacturing history of notebooks

context: Which choice best describes a key difference between how the author of Passage A and the author of Passage B view the friction involved in handwriting?

choices.text: The author of Passage A views the friction as a minor inconvenience, while the author of Passage B views it as the primary reason to keep a journal at all.
Both authors agree that the friction of handwriting is the single most important factor in choosing a journaling method.
The author of Passage A dismisses the friction entirely, while the author of Passage B considers it essential.

why.B: Passage B explicitly downplays friction as 'not obviously a virtue,' so the two authors do not agree here
why.C: Passage A does not dismiss the friction - the author explicitly values it; this distractor swaps the two authors' views

context: Based on both passages, the author of Passage B would most likely respond to Passage A's claim that a notebook 'is a room with one door' by arguing that—

choices.text: a single, fixed location for a thought is a limitation, not an advantage, since most thoughts belong in more than one context.
a notebook's single location makes it more secure from accidental deletion than any digital system.
a room with one door is an accurate description of how digital note systems also function.
the comparison to a room is unfair because notebooks do not actually resemble rooms in any way.

context: What most directly leads Renata to try oiling the gear housing rather than attempting some other repair?

choices.text: Written instructions Master Okafor had taped inside the lamp room door.
A suggestion radioed in from the harbor office during the storm.
A similar repair she had already performed alone earlier that same night.
Her memory of watching Master Okafor use thinned reservoir oil to ease a swollen metal part in October.

why.D: The passage states plainly that what she had was the memory of Master Okafor's October repair with thinned oil, which she then applies to the gear.

why.B: no radio contact occurs anywhere in the passage

context: Based on the passage, what causes a translation choice that once sounded neutral to eventually sound archaic or unintentionally comic?

choices.text: The original novel's plot becomes less relevant to contemporary readers.
Later translators deliberately introduce comic errors to critique earlier versions.
The target language keeps changing over time while the translation's word choices remain fixed.
Publishers edit older translations without updating their original publication dates.

why.C: The third paragraph explains that words drift in register over time, so a translation calibrated to an earlier register can come to sound archaic or comic as the living language moves on without it.
why.A: the passage discusses language drift, not the plot's relevance
why.B: no such deliberate critique is described in the passage
why.D: not mentioned anywhere in the passage

context: What most directly causes Mireille to finally tell Master Alduin about the error, after having already decided to say nothing?

choices.text: Master Alduin's direct request that she double-check her soundings before he signed the chart.
Learning from the clerk that a ship had been lost near Cormorant Point on an improperly charted reef.
Her fear that she would be dismissed the way the journeyman had been two winters earlier.
The shipping company's deadline for delivering the finished chart.

why.B: The passage states plainly that it was the clerk's mention of the vessel lost eleven years earlier that changed Mireille's mind, giving the abstract quarter-mile error real, human stakes.

why.C: this fear is part of why she initially says nothing, not why she changes her mind
why.D: no deadline is mentioned as a cause of her decision

context: Based on the passage, what most directly causes some large time banks to 'stall,' as the passage describes it?

choices.text: Members begin demanding cash payment instead of hourly credit once the bank grows large.
The bank's administrators run out of hours to allocate to new members.
Licensed tradespeople refuse to participate once a bank exceeds a certain size.
Supply and demand for different kinds of labor fail to match, so a member needing one kind of help can't find it even though the ledger shows available hours.

why.B: administrators allocating hours to new members is not described as a mechanism
why.C: the passage discusses licensed trades only as a category some banks exclude from the start, not tradespeople leaving due to size

context: Based on the passage, why does a serotinous cone opening at a lower heat threshold, after a milder fire, put its seed at a disadvantage?

The seed would fall onto ash too nutrient-rich for a young seedling to tolerate.
The seed would be exposed to browsing animals before the fire had passed completely.
The seed would land on ground still shaded by a canopy that the milder fire failed to clear, leaving it unable to compete for sunlight.

why.A: the passage never claims a seed released this way cannot germinate
why.B: the passage describes nutrient-rich ash as beneficial, not harmful, to germinating seeds
why.C: the passage attributes protection from browsing animals to litter being burned away, not to timing relative to browsing animals

context: According to the passage, what specifically caused the lamp's beam to slow from its normal four-second interval?

choices.text: The reservoir had run low on oil, weakening the flame's brightness.
A gear tooth in the clockwork housing had worn thin and begun to slip instead of catch.
High winds had cracked the lamp room's glass, letting rain into the mechanism.

indifferent to a technical dispute with no practical stakes.

why.A: Correct — the author writes that "None of this means the number is worthless" and then insists it is "a conclusion, not an observation."
why.B: The author explicitly rejects the reading that the fieldwork was careless.
why.C: Acoustics is said to establish where whales are, while counting "remains unsolved for this species."
why.D: The final sentence stresses that the stakes are enormous if the number is wrong.

context: The phrase "somewhere uncomfortable and honest" conveys the author's view that the field has:

choices.text: gained real knowledge while becoming more candid about what it still cannot measure.
reached an impasse that makes further research difficult to justify.
allowed political pressure to distort what it reports publicly.
abandoned ship surveys in favor of a method it does not fully trust.

why.A: Correct — the sentence that follows says the field knows more about where the whales are and not much more about how many, which is exactly a gain paired with an admitted limit.
why.B: The passage describes acoustics as an advance, not a dead end.
why.C: No political distortion of reported results is suggested; managers use the best available number openly.
why.D: Nothing indicates ship surveys have been abandoned.

context: The comparison of the survey effort to something that "would embarrass a pollster" is used to:

choices.text: convey how small the sample is relative to the area it is meant to represent.
suggest that whale researchers lack training in statistical sampling.
imply that public opinion polling is a more rigorous discipline.
criticize the funding agencies that limit time at sea.

why.A: Correct — the clause is immediately followed by the scale of the mismatch: a handful of ships and a few weeks against an ocean the size of a continent.
why.B: The next paragraph attributes the limitation to arithmetic rather than to the researchers' skill.
why.C: Polling is invoked as a familiar yardstick for sample size, not held up as superior.
why.D: Funding is never mentioned in the passage.

context: Which detail most directly supports the claim that exhaustive ship-based counting is impractical?

choices.text: Covering the eastern North Pacific with one vessel would take roughly forty years.
The most cited figure is around thirty animals.
Right whales gather where their prey gathers.
A moored recorder can listen for a year rather than a few weeks.

why.A: Correct — a survey that outlasts the population it measures is the passage's direct demonstration that the approach cannot work.
why.B: The figure is the disputed output of the method, not evidence about its feasibility.
why.C: Uneven distribution undermines an assumption in the reasoning, but it does not speak to how long a survey would take.
why.D: This describes the advantage of the alternative method rather than the limits of the ship-based one.

context: Which detail best supports the claim that acoustic monitoring has genuinely added to what researchers know?

choices.text: Recorders have shown right whales present in parts of the Bering Sea in months no survey has covered.
Right whales call, and recorders can operate in darkness and fog.
A hundred calls may come from one talkative animal or from twenty quiet ones.
A responsible estimate is published as a range spanning roughly a factor of three.

why.A: Correct — this is a specific fact established by recorders that no previous method had produced.
why.B: This explains why recorders are capable, which is a precondition for the finding rather than the finding itself.
why.C: This states a limitation of acoustics, not a contribution.
why.D: The published range describes the uncertainty of the ship-based estimate and predates the acoustic work.

context: Which detail most directly supports the idea that the assumption about how whales distribute themselves is imperfect?

choices.text: Whales gather where their prey gathers, and prey is not evenly distributed either.
A whale must be at the surface in order to be seen.
Detection rates are measured in conditions unlike those of an actual survey.
Distinguishing individual whales by voice remains unsolved.

why.A: Correct — the passage names this as the reason the even-distribution assumption is "false in detail."
why.B: Surfacing time affects whether an animal is visible, a separate link in the chain.
why.C: Detection rates concern the observer's reliability, not how whales are spread across the ocean.
why.D: This is a limitation of acoustics and unrelated to the distribution assumption.

context: In describing the cabinets as "a museum with no curator," the narrator most nearly means that the contents were:

choices.text: carefully preserved by someone who was no longer there to explain them
valuable enough that a museum would have wanted to acquire them
neglected for years and left in disorder
arranged deliberately for visitors to walk through and admire

why.A: Correct — the museum half of the comparison captures the deliberate order the narrator finds, while the missing curator captures the absence of the one person who could say what any of it meant.
why.B: The comparison is about how the objects were kept, not what they were worth; nothing suggests the flour tins and buttons had market value.
why.C: This ignores the museum half entirely. The narrator finds flour in labeled tins and buttons sorted by color, which is the opposite of disorder.
why.D: Perpetua lived alone and kept the cabinets for herself. The comparison points to preservation, not display.

context: The narrator's comparison of the house to a shell, "the way a shell is a container for whatever lives inside it," functions in the passage to:

choices.text: state a belief the narrator goes on to reverse
explain why the house was built the way it was
emphasize how fragile the old house had become
suggest that Perpetua felt trapped in the house

why.A: Correct — the narrator introduces the shell comparison as what she "had believed" and immediately says she had it backward: Perpetua was keeping the house, not being kept by it.
why.B: The comparison describes a relationship between person and house, not architecture or construction.
why.C: Shells can suggest fragility, but the narrator uses this one for the idea of containing, and the house in this passage is anything but delicate.
why.D: The passage reverses the containment idea rather than developing it into confinement; Perpetua is shown as the active keeper.

context: The phrase "that thin, upright script that leaned into the wind of the page" characterizes Perpetua's handwriting as:

choices.text: narrow and slanted, as though pressing forward against resistance
faded by age to the point of near illegibility
hurried and careless, made without attention
unusually large and looping across the paper

why.A: Correct — thin and upright describe the letters themselves, and leaning into a wind supplies the slant along with a sense of effort directed against something.
why.B: Nothing in the description concerns fading or legibility; the narrator reads the labels without difficulty.
why.C: Labeled tins and sorted buttons establish care, and an upright script leaning deliberately is not a careless one.
why.D: Thin and upright are the opposite of large and looping.

context: The narrator compares the six wooden spoons to "a set of parentheses waiting for something to enclose" primarily to convey that the spoons:

choices.text: share a matching curve that now surrounds nothing
were kept as a complete set and never separated
had been damaged in a way that made them unusable
were arranged in pairs rather than as a group of six

why.A: Correct — the spoons are all worn on one side and curved the same direction, and parentheses that enclose nothing carry the sense of something absent, which the closing paragraph confirms when they sit in a drawer "still waiting."
why.B: That the set is complete is stated plainly elsewhere; the comparison is doing the work of shape and absence, not of completeness.
why.C: The wear is evidence of long use, and the narrator keeps and stores them, so usability is not the point.
why.D: Parentheses come in pairs, but the narrator describes all six laid side by side, not sorted into pairs.

context: By describing her mother's reaction as "a small exhale that in our family does the work of an entire paragraph," the narrator suggests that:

choices.text: a wordless sound communicates a great deal among people who know each other well
her mother had been rehearsing a long speech about the house
her mother was too out of breath from other work to say much
the family prefers writing to speaking when a subject is difficult

why.A: Correct — the sound is small, the narrator recognizes it immediately, and its stated effect is that of a paragraph, so brevity is carrying a large amount of shared meaning.
why.B: Her mother's actual words are two short remarks; nothing suggests a prepared speech.
why.C: An exhale here is an expressive sound, not a sign of physical exertion, and the phone call gives no hint of either.
why.D: The comparison to a paragraph is a measure of how much is conveyed, not a claim about a preference for writing.

context: The statement that "Perpetua's English arrived late and never fully unpacked" treats her language as though it were:

choices.text: a traveler who came to stay but never quite settled in
a skill she abandoned before completing it
a possession she deliberately kept hidden from her family
a burden she was forced to carry against her will

why.A: Correct — arriving and unpacking belong to someone who travels to a new place, and the sentence goes on to describe sentences that "took the long way around," extending the same idea.
why.B: She used English daily in speech and writing, so the comparison is about how it settled rather than whether she stopped learning.
why.C: Nothing suggests concealment; the narrator reads her labels and recipe cards freely.
why.D: Unpacking implies arrival and settling, not compulsion, and the passage treats her English with affection rather than resentment.

context: The narrator describes the evening light as moving "the way water finds the low places" in order to emphasize the light's:

choices.text: slow, unhurried spread across the room
unusual coldness at the end of the day
tendency to damage the old floorboards
sudden appearance after a long absence

why.A: Correct — the sentence already says the light came across the floorboards slowly, and water settling into low ground is a gradual, inevitable motion that reinforces it.
why.B: The comparison is to how water moves, not to how water feels; temperature is not at issue.
why.C: Water can damage floors, but the point of comparison here is the manner of the movement, and nothing in the passage reports damage.
why.D: Finding the low places is a gradual process, the opposite of a sudden arrival.

context: The assertion that "an empty house is heavier than a full one" is best understood as:

choices.text: a deliberate paradox in which weight stands for emotional difficulty
a literal observation about how sound carries in a bare room
an exaggeration the narrator immediately admits is untrue
a practical warning about the labor of moving furniture

why.A: Correct — the claim contradicts ordinary sense, and the sentences that follow relocate the weight to "somewhere harder to carry," which makes the burden felt rather than physical.
why.B: Acoustics never come up, and the narrator ties the heaviness to what packing removes, not to what a bare room sounds like.
why.C: She does not retract it; she elaborates on it, saying the three-quarters-boxed kitchen pressed on her more than before.
why.D: The labor of packing is real in the passage, but the narrator's point is that the room grew heavier as it emptied, which no amount of lifting explains.

context: The passage's closing image, in which the narrator hears the third stair "clearing its throat," achieves its effect by:

choices.text: returning to the house's voice from the opening paragraph and treating it as still speaking
revealing that the narrator has moved back into her grandmother's house
suggesting that the narrator has begun to doubt her own memory
introducing a new character who has been listening from the stairs

why.A: Correct — the opening gives the house creaks, drafts, and a groan from the third stair, and the ending gives that same stair a throat to clear, so the house is still addressing her from forty miles away.
why.B: She says the spoons are in a drawer in her own kitchen and the stair is forty miles off, so she has not returned.
why.C: The image is presented as something she hears rather than something she questions, and nothing casts doubt on her recollection.
why.D: No person is introduced; the sound belongs to the stair, which the passage has treated as part of the house's voice from the first paragraph.

context: Nadia's reaction to her brother's age is compared to being startled "the way you are startled by your own voice on a recording" in order to suggest that she finds the fact:

choices.text: familiar and strange at the same time, because it concerns her as much as him
embarrassing to admit to anyone outside the family
impossible to believe without seeing documentation
less important than the other changes she has been through

why.A: Correct — a recorded voice is unmistakably your own and still sounds wrong, and Amir turning forty-four means Nadia is aging too, so the comparison folds her into the surprise.
why.B: The comparison concerns a private jolt of recognition, and nothing in the scene suggests she is worried about outside opinion.
why.C: The narrator says she keeps forgetting and being startled, not that she doubts the fact.
why.D: The passage lists her own changes separately; this comparison is about the shock itself, not about ranking it below anything.

context: In writing that the clove cigarettes their father quit in 1998 left a smell "whose ghost had never left the front room," the narrator conveys that:

choices.text: a trace of him persists in the house long after the habit ended
the family believes the house is genuinely haunted
their father continued smoking in secret for years afterward
the front room has been sealed off and left unused

why.A: Correct — calling the lingering smell a ghost makes it a remnant that outlasts its source, which fits a habit abandoned decades earlier and still faintly detectable.
why.B: The word is figurative; the passage treats the smell as a physical trace, and no character suggests a haunting.
why.C: The passage gives 1998 as the year he quit and offers nothing to undercut it.
why.D: Nadia stands in the entryway and the room is part of the house they are sorting, so it is not sealed off.

context: The narrator writes that "The arithmetic of it had never balanced" to describe the relationship between Nadia and Amir. This figure of speech emphasizes that:

choices.text: the two siblings contributed to their father unequally, and both knew it
the siblings disagreed about how much the house was worth
Nadia had sent less money than she had promised to send
their father had divided his property unfairly between them

why.A: Correct — the sentence follows a list of what Amir did over eleven years against what Nadia did, and the accounting image names the imbalance they both recognized and never discussed.
why.B: Valuation never comes up; the imbalance described is one of time and presence.
why.C: The passage says she sent money and called on birthdays without suggesting she fell short of a promise.
why.D: The figure describes what the siblings gave, not what their father left behind.

context: The maple in the side yard, remembered as "a stick of a thing tied to a stake" and now tall enough to shade the house, most likely functions as:

choices.text: a measure of how much time has passed since the family arrived
evidence that the property has been poorly maintained
a sign that Nadia intends to sell the house quickly
a reminder of an argument the siblings had as children

why.A: Correct — Nadia remembers it being planted the spring after they arrived, so its growth from a staked stick to full shade marks the same span the photograph and her father's 1971 arrival establish.
why.B: A tree that has grown tall enough to shade a wall is a sign of years passing, not of neglect.
why.C: Her plans for the house are left unresolved, and the tree is tied to memory rather than to any decision.
why.D: No argument involving the tree is mentioned; what she recalls is its planting.

context: The narrator describes the bakery's finances as "a slow leak she had mistaken for a business." This comparison is used to:

choices.text: capture the harshness of the judgment the narrator made at nineteen
explain a physical problem with the bakery building
show that Mr. Callan shared the narrator's view of the loan
present the mother's own assessment of what she was doing

why.A: Correct — the phrase comes from the speech the narrator delivered in the car at nineteen while having opinions, and the rest of the passage is spent revising it.
why.B: The leak is figurative, standing for money steadily lost; no damage to the building is mentioned.
why.C: Mr. Callan grants the loan every year and speaks of what the town needs, so he does not treat it as a mistake.
why.D: The mother answers that she is not arguing with the arithmetic but also counting other things, which is a different assessment from the narrator's.

context: Mr. Callan says the town needs "somewhere that smells like something in February." He uses this phrasing to identify the bakery as:

choices.text: a source of ordinary comfort during the emptiest part of the year
the only building in town with working heat in winter
a business that could attract tourists earlier in the season
a place whose ventilation problems the town had long tolerated

why.A: Correct — February falls in the months the passage describes as emptied of everyone but the crews and the eleven families, and naming a smell rather than a product makes the bakery a comfort rather than a transaction.
why.B: He speaks of smell, not warmth, and no comparison between buildings is made.
why.C: His remark is about the off-season itself; the passage treats summer tourists as a separate matter the loan cannot fix.
why.D: The smell he names is the appeal of the place, not a defect.

context: The narrator writes that on the drive home his mother "let me sit with it for about ten miles." Measuring the pause this way primarily conveys:

choices.text: that she allowed a long silence to pass before responding
that the two of them were lost and driving without direction
that she was concentrating too hard on the road to speak
that the argument continued for most of the drive

why.A: Correct — the drive is forty minutes each way, so ten miles of it is a substantial stretch, and giving the silence a distance rather than a duration stresses how long she let it run.
why.B: The route is a familiar annual one between Wexford and home, and no confusion about direction is suggested.
why.C: The passage attributes the silence to her deliberate choice, introduced by her letting him sit with it.
why.D: The narrator had already finished speaking before this pause; what fills the ten miles is silence, not argument.
